result.eventTitle: AMD Fiscal Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results

data.text: Welcome to the AMD third quarter, 2026 conference call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question and answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. And please note that this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Matt Ramsey, VP Financial Strategy, NIR. Thank you, Matt. You may begin.

Thank you, and welcome to AMD's third quarter, 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. By now, you should have had the opportunity to review a copy of our earnings press release and the accompanying slides. If you have not had the chance to review these materials, they can be found on the Investor Relations page of AMD.com. We will refer primarily to non-GAAP financial measures during today's call. The full non-GAAP-to-GAAP reconciliations are available in today's press release and slides posted on our website. Participants on today's conference call include Dr. Lisa Su, our Chair and CEO, and Jean Hu, Executive Vice President, CFO, and Treasurer. This is a live call and will be replayed via webcast on our website. Before we begin, I would like to note that AMD will participate in the following events with the financial community this quarter. The UBS Technology and AI Conference on Tuesday, December 1st, and Barclays' 24th Annual Global Technology Conference on Wednesday, December 9th. Today's discussion contains forward-looking statements based on our current beliefs, assumptions, and expectations, including forward-looking statements regarding financial projections, business and industry trends that speak only as of today and as such involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from our current expectations. Please refer to the cautionary statement in our press release for more information on the factors that could cause actual results to differ materially. With that, I will hand the call over to Lisa.

Thank you, Matt, and good afternoon to all those listening today. The third quarter was the largest and most profitable in our history as we began ramping our next-generation data center products. Revenue increased 45% year-over-year to $13.4 billion, driven by record Epic and Instinct sales and strong embedded growth. Earnings per share grew even faster, increasing 74% to $2.09. We executed very well in the quarter, with Helios production ramping as planned and Epic adoption expanding across cloud, enterprise, and superintelligence workloads. Data center revenue growth has accelerated sequentially every quarter this year, with the segment contributing 64% of total revenue in the third quarter, up from 47% just one year ago. We expect that acceleration to continue in the fourth quarter, driven by increased demand for inference and agentic workloads and the ramp of our newest products. Turning to our segments. Data center revenue grew 97% year-over-year to a record $8.5 billion. In server, both cloud and enterprise sales more than doubled year-over-year. We significantly exceeded our previous outlook of more than 80% growth as we gained revenue share. Customers deployed Epic across more applications with agentic workloads contributing significant growth. In cloud, hyperscalers deployed substantial volumes of Epic servers in the quarter to run more internal services and expand their public cloud offerings. Curran is now the most widely deployed Epic generation in the public cloud, with more than 540 instance types available globally from the largest providers. Cloud providers also added significant EPIC capacity in the quarter for personal and enterprise agents, which are quickly becoming the next killer app for CPUs in the cloud. Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots illustrate how quickly personal agents are growing, with more than 10 million people activating Muse agents in the first six weeks. Enterprises are moving fast as well, putting agents to work across software development, supply chain, and IT operations. These agents work continuously and in parallel across applications and enterprise systems, adding to accelerator demand, while creating a substantial increase in CPU demand. Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work. In head nodes, we won major deployments with several of the largest model developers and cloud providers in the quarter, which will ramp over the coming quarters. EPIC's leadership performance and mature ecosystem, proven at scale, have made it the host CPU of choice for custom accelerators. As one example, OpenAI selected Turin EPIC processors as the host CPUs for its first custom accelerator platforms. In enterprise, EPIC's server sell-through was a record with strong demand from new and existing customers. We added dozens of first-time EPIC customers in the quarter, including large financial services, communications, retail, and healthcare companies. Existing customers are also making EPIC their primary compute platform, extending adoption from specific workloads to a much larger share of their overall infrastructure. We began revenue shipments of EPIC Venice processors in the third quarter, and the first OEM systems are on track for availability this quarter. Early demand is the strongest we have seen for any new EPIC generation. Our OEM and ODM partners have committed more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than Turin, and cloud providers are deploying Venice this quarter ahead of instance rollouts planned for early 2027. We recently launched Helion, a Venice reference design that enables turnkey EPIC rack-scale systems for Argentic infrastructure. Customers can configure Helion for their workloads, from all CPU racks for hyperscalers to enterprise systems combining VENIS and Instinct GPUs that can run agents and models together. In the all CPU configuration, a single Helion rack has up to 144 VENIS processors with nearly 74,000 threads, delivering the highest agent density in the industry. Every major server OEM and ODM plans to offer Helion, with the first systems shipping this quarter. Looking more broadly, demand for server compute is accelerating across cloud, enterprise, agentic, and superintelligence infrastructure. EPIC is the industry's broadest portfolio spanning all of these markets, with per-socket leadership for cloud and agents, Her core leadership for enterprise and head nodes, and memory and I.O. options tuned to each workload. Venice builds on that leadership with significantly better performance per watt, performance per core, and performance per dollar than any other x86 or ARM server CPU, positioning us to gain share and significantly grow our server business as the TAM grows to approximately $220 billion by 2030. Turning to our data center AI business. Frontier Labs, hyperscalers, and cloud providers expanded instinct deployments for inferencing and training, driving record revenue. We started shipping MI455X in volume in the quarter, and lead customers, including Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle, brought their first Helio racks online quickly. Customers are now running their latest models and workloads on Helios, and we are seeing very strong performance with the initial deployments. We expect Helios deployments to increase substantially in the fourth quarter as production continues to ramp and HPE, Dell, Lenovo, Supermicro, and other OEM and ODM partners begin shipping systems. We are very pleased with the overall performance we are seeing at the rack level. MI-455X leads in compute flops, memory capacity, and scale-out bandwidth. And as Helios comes to market, it delivers an even larger lead in memory bandwidth and higher scale-up bandwidth than the competition. We are working closely with our manufacturing and OEM partners to scale production as customers expand their deployments. In supercomputing, EuroHPC selected Instinct MI430X GPUs and 6-Gen EPIC processors for Lumi AI, Europe's next flagship supercomputer, planned to come online in the second half of 2027. MI430X delivers nearly nine times the double-precision performance of the competition, which is critical for scientific simulations. As a result, MI430X has now been selected to power next-generation systems around the world, and we are well-positioned to win additional designs as governments and research centers plan their next major investments. In software, we launched ROCCM 10 with major enhancements for production deployments at scale, including faster startup across large GPU clusters and greater resilience for long-running workloads. Rackham 10 also adds agentic performance tuning with Rackham.ai, which profiles workloads, identifies bottlenecks, and applies and validates improvements, turning weeks of engineering optimization into hours. Customers are also using their own agents to optimize models on our open software stack. For example, Anthropic highlighted that one engineer used Claude to bring up their latest model on Instinct MI-355x racks over a single weekend with strong performance. Our work with Frontier Labs is already enabling their models to handle complex software development and performance tuning for Instinct. And as those capabilities continue to improve, the benefits extend to everyone in the AMD ecosystem. We announced two acquisitions in the quarter to strengthen our superintelligence portfolio. TALIS brings a highly experienced engineering team and specialized silicon built for low-latency, efficient inference. We plan to integrate their technology across our solutions portfolio to address the growing demand for low-latency superintelligence applications. World Labs, led by co-founder and CEO Dr. Fei-Fei Li, brings a world-class research team with expertise in spatial intelligence and models that understand the physical world, giving us deeper insight into how frontier models and workloads are evolving. Fei-Fei will join AMD as chief scientist, leading our model research and helping shape our future hardware, software, and systems roadmaps. We expect both acquisitions to close by the end of the year. Looking ahead, our focus is on execution at scale. The ramps of Venice, the MI450 series, and Helios are still early, and all three are on track to grow significantly. We now expect data center segment revenue growth to accelerate in the fourth quarter, and full year segment revenue to more than double from 2025. Our visibility into 2027 also continues to strengthen. Last quarter, we said we expected annual server revenue to grow more than 70% and data center segment revenue to more than double for the year. Since then, customers have expanded their Epic and Instinct deployment plans, and we have secured more supply to support that growth. We now expect server revenue to double year-over-year in 2027 and data center AI revenue to grow even faster than we projected 90 days ago. As a result, we expect Datacenter to be more than 80% of our total revenue in 2027 and to drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth. Looking further out, customer engagements for MI500 continue to progress very well. Interest is very high as it is another significant leap forward in performance. We are working very closely with multiple Frontier Labs to optimize MI500 for their workloads as they plan multi-gigawatt deployments. Turning to client and gaming, segment revenue decreased 8% year-over-year to $3.7 billion. In client, revenue increased 7% year-over-year to $2.9 billion, driven by strong sales of our Ryzen mobile processors. Commercial is becoming a larger part of our client business, as large enterprises adopt Ryzen Pro PCs across their employee base. Eight of the ten largest banks in the world and seven of the ten largest healthcare and automotive companies now use Ryzen Pro PCs. OEMs continue expanding their AMD-based commercial lineups from everyday business PCs to high-end workstations. HP, Lenovo, and others launched the first commercial notebooks and small form factor desktops, featuring our newest Ryzen AI Max Pro 400 series processors. These systems deliver workstation class performance and run superintelligence models with up to 300 billion parameters locally. Looking at the market, PC sell-throughs slowed late in the quarter as higher memory and component costs weighed on demand. We are managing the business accordingly, aligning sell-in with sell-through, to keep customer and channel inventory healthy. In 2027, we are planning for PC market unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage. In this environment, we expect to outperform the market as we deliver our Ryzen roadmap and grow our commercial footprint. In gaming, revenue declined 40% year-over-year to $773 million, primarily due to lower semi-custom sales as expected at this stage of the console cycle. Gaming graphics revenue declined year-over-year, while Radeon GPU channel sell-through increased sequentially. Beyond gaming, Radeon AI Pro revenue grew significantly from the prior quarter as more developers choose AMD to run and fine-tune models locally. We expect strong growth for Radeon AI Pro to continue, driven by our leadership performance per dollar and an open software stack optimized for the latest open source models. Turning for our embedded segment, revenue increased 29% year-over-year to $1.1 billion, the fourth consecutive quarter of accelerating growth. Demand was very strong across all of our end markets, led by strong growth with aerospace and defense, automotive, communications, and industrial customers. Data center buildouts are also driving higher demand for our embedded CPUs and adaptive SOCs in control plane and optical networking applications. We remain on track to close more than 18 billion of design wins in 2026, our third consecutive record year. Adaptive design wins have increased every year since we acquired Xilinx, with embedded x86 and semi-custom wins growing even faster. As these wins ramp over the next few years, we expect our embedded business to deliver strong double-digit annual revenue growth and continue outgrowing the market. In summary, we delivered an excellent third quarter and expect an even stronger fourth quarter as data center and embedded segment growth more than offsets lower client CPU sales. We entered 2027 with the strongest product portfolio in our history and significant customer momentum. We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year. Based on our current visibility, we now expect revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027, which is more than twice the long-term financial model we outlined at our Financial Analyst Day last November. Data Center will be the largest contributor, driven by expanding Helios deployments and continued Epic ShareGates. We also expect embedded growth to accelerate next year, driven by adoption of our adoptive and x86 solutions. Beyond 2027, we are increasing R&D investment across our silicon, software, and systems roadmaps and working closely with our largest customers to support their ambitious infrastructure plans for the next three to five years. We are also deepening our collaboration with our supply chain partners and investing alongside them to secure the long-term capacity our growth will require. Taken together, these give us strong confidence in our ability to sustain exceptional revenue growth for years to come, with earnings growing even faster. Now, I will turn the call over to Jean to provide additional color on our third quarter results. Jean?

Thank you, Lisa, and good afternoon, everyone. I'll start with the review of our financial results and then provide our outlook for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. We delivered an outstanding third quarter. Revenue increased 45 percent year-over-year to a record $13.4 billion, exceeding the high end of our guidance, driven by our data center segment, which nearly doubled year-over-year. Revenue increased 16 percent sequentially, driven by strong growth in the data center and embedded segments, partially offset by decline in the client and the gaming segment. Our data center segment accounted for approximately 64% of total revenue, up from 58% last quarter, underscoring the continued shift in our business mix and its increasing contribution to AMD's growth. Growth margin was 56%, up 190 basis points year-over-year, reflecting a richer product mix. Operating expenses were $3.6 billion, an increase of 29% year-of-year, as we continue to invest in R&D to expand our data center silicon systems and software capabilities. Operating income grew 75% year-of-year to a record $3.9 billion, significantly outpacing our revenue growth. Operating margin was 29%, expanding more than five percentage points year-for-year, underscoring the operating leverage in the business as we scale. In the third quarter, we began recognizing the counting impact of warrants issued under our previously announced customer agreement as we shipped MI450 series GPUs. Our gap diluted earnings per share were $1.46. which included 1.1 billion non-cash charge in other income and expense, primarily reflecting the increase in our share price and the changes in the estimated probability of meeting the warrant conditions. Going forward, this quarterly non-cash fare value adjustment I expect to As we and our customers progress under this agreement. The amounts will vary each quarter based on AMD's stock price and other valuation assumptions. These non-cash adjustments will not affect our non-GAAP results or free cash flow. Our non-GAAP diluted earnings per share was $2.09. Now, turning to our reportable segment, starting with the data center. Data center segment revenue was a record of $8.5 billion, up 97% year-over-year, driven by record server revenue on strong demand for our fifth-generation EPIC processors, and by record data center AI revenue, highlighted by the launch of our AMD Instinct MI450 series GPUs. On a sequential basis, data center revenue increased to 27 percent. Primarily driven by initial MI450 series sales and a strong server revenue growth, the data center segment operating income was $2.9 billion, up 168% year-over-year, and the operating margin increased to 34% compared to 25% a year ago, demonstrating strong operating leverage of the data center business. Client on the gaming segment revenue was $3.7 billion, down 8% year-for-year due to lower semi-customer and graphic sales, partially offset by higher demand for the latest generation Ryzen mobile processors. In the client business, revenue was $2.9 billion, up 7% year-for-year, driven by higher sales of Ryzen mobile processors. Sequentially, client revenue was down 4% as higher memory cost weighted on PC unit demand partially offset by a richer mix of high-end processors. Gaming revenue was $773 million, down 40% year-for-year due to lower semi-customer revenue and lower graphics demand. Sequentially, gaming revenue was essentially flat. Client and gaming segment operating income was $573 million, or 15% of revenue, compared to $867 million, or 21% a year ago. Embedded segment revenue was $1.1 billion, up 29% year-over-year and 14% sequentially, as demand strengthened across several end markets, led by growth in aerospace and defense, automotive, communication, and the industrial end markets. Embedded segment operating income was $453 million, or 41% of revenue. Compared to $283 million, or 33% a year ago. Turning to balance sheet and cash flow. During the quarter, inventory increased approximately $3 billion sequentially to $11.5 billion to fulfill our strong data center demand. We generated $1.2 billion in cash from operating activities of continuing operations. Free cash flow was $554 million, reflecting increased working capital investment and ongoing capital expenditures to secure equipment and capacity for the rapid growth of our data center business, including back-end capacity dedicated to support our data center demand. We expect to continue to invest in inventory and capacity to support our strong growth in 2027. At the end of the quarter, cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investment were $15.8 billion. Our total debt was $7.1 billion, including $4.75 billion senior notes offering We completed it in August. Now, turning to our fourth quarter, 2026 outlook. We expect revenue to be approximately $17 billion, plus or minus 3%. The middle point of our guidance represents approximately 66% year-of-year revenue growth, primarily driven by the acceleration of our data center segment. Sequentially, we expect revenue to grow by approximately 27%, driven by a sharp increase in our data center segment of approximately 50% growth, a decline in our client and gaming segment of greater than 20%, and a double-digit growth in our embedded segment. In addition, we expect the fourth quarter non-GAAP gross margin to be approximately 55%, and we expect non-GAAP operating expenses to be approximately 3.75 billion. We expect non-GAAP net interest and other expenses to be, again, of approximately 4 million. We expect our non-GAAP effective tax rate to be 13%. And diluted share count is expected to be approximately 1.67 billion shares, including the estimated impact of closing the TALUS and the World Labs acquisition in the fourth quarter. We're not expecting our fourth quarter share count to be impacted by customer warrants. In closing, the third quarter was an outstanding quarter for AMD with record revenue, significant operating margin expansion, and earnings growth, reflecting disciplined execution across the business. As our data center business continues to scale, we are very well positioned to drive increased profitability and long-term shareholder value. With that, I'll turn it back to Matt for the Q&A session.
Thank you very much.

Thank you. We will now be conducting a question and answer session. We ask that you please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate that your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you'd like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. One moment, please, while we poll for questions. And the first question comes from the line of Tom O'Malley with Barclays. Please proceed with your question.

Hey, good evening, and thanks for taking my question. Congrats on the great results. I guess, Lisa, let's start off with the fact that you're giving some more color into 2027. It looks like revenue is growing 80%, but the data center component of that is growing much faster, where data center is going to be greater than 80% of your business next year. So maybe can you talk about first and foremost, like, is this backed up by supply, whether that be wafers, packaging, substrate, memory? And then if you look at the demand profile behind that, would demand outstrip that supply if you were able to get some more? Thank you.

Yeah, sure, Tom. Thanks for the question. So look, we have a lot of momentum going into the fourth quarter and into 2027. We do see a situation where there is very strong demand. So we see demand across the data center business, across our CPU business, as well as our data center AI business. And when you look at the rate and pace of that growth, we've been planning for it for the last several years. So we've absolutely spent a significant amount of time with our customers planning what their needs are in terms of their deployments and their deployment schedules, and also with our supply chain partners to ensure that we have the wafers, the substrates, the advanced packaging, the memory, all of the other components that go along with it. It is true that demand is higher than supply, so we continue to work with our supply chain partners to increase supply, and I do believe that there is a good opportunity for us to do that, just given the strong relationships we have throughout the ecosystem. But sitting where we are today, to be able to say that the overall company will grow greater than 80%, especially the server business will approximately double from a fairly high point in 2026, and then the data center AI business, we continue to have strong visibility, and we see strong demand from our customers, and we continue to see also good follow-through on all of the other aspects of the infrastructure that are needed. So overall, we're very positive about the data center growth into 2027.

Super helpful. And then just as a follow-up on the client side, you're saying down greater than 20% in the fourth quarter. That's kind of in line with what we've heard from others so far in the market. But if you look at 27, I think something that's difficult is that normally you see seasonality down in Q1, and then you wouldn't get a recovery until Q2, Q3. So maybe talk about what the longevity of this correction kind of looks like and why you've been able to kind of outperform a bit up until this point and how you see that kind of coming out of this trough into next year. Thanks, Lisa.

Yeah, sure, Tom. So I'm talking a little bit about the PC market. The PC market continues to be an important market to us. I think we were signaling all along in the last couple of calls that we were expecting a sub-seasonal second half of the year, and that's how it's played out. Our view is this is one of those times when component prices go up. It affects overall system pricing. One would expect the consumer markets to be more sensitive to that, and so we have seen a bit of slowdown in the sell-through. We're just managing the business very prudently, and we want to ensure that inventory stays healthy throughout the channel and throughout our customers. And so our planning assumption for 2027 is that the market will be double-digit percentage down. We will certainly focus on the segments where we can add the most value, places like enterprise where we continue to be underrepresented, premium consumer, desktop channel. These are really good markets for us, but we are planning with the current environment for a down year for 2027, and we will work through that. The good part about it is our supply chain is quite fungible across our PC business and our data center business, and so that actually does afford us the ability to move supply around as we see these signals in the market, and overall, as I said earlier, we do have more demand than we have supply, and so we're continuing to work all of the aspects to increase supply as we go through the next few quarters.
Thank you. And the next question comes from the line of Vivek Aria with Bank of America Securities. Please proceed with your question.

Thanks for taking my questions. Lisa, you know, there's a lot of market debate about the financing of data centers and availability of land, power, and shell, et cetera. So kind of a two-parter, what's the level of confidence, right, that AMD has that your anchor customers have the financing and the physical infrastructure to support, I think it's roughly three gigawatt or so of planned AMD deployments into 27? And then as we look beyond, you know, many of your competitors are kind of investing in the ecosystem, providing residual value guarantees and such, and saying there is a lot more fungibility of their products. So does that create kind of a competitive dynamic for AMD? So just curious to hear your perspective on 27 readiness and 28 competitive landscape.

Sure, Vivek. Thanks for the question. So, as I said earlier, we're seeing very strong demand from our, you know, lead data center AI customers. I think, you know, you can see that there's a strong demand for more compute, and MI-455 is positioned extremely well. When we look at, you know, Venice, MI-455, Helios, I think we feel extremely good about the competitiveness. We have been planning for this ramp with our customers jointly, so we have good visibility into the 2027, as you said, land, power, shells, all of those, the data center infrastructure, and we are very much working hand-in-hand with our customers, so we know where the GPUs are going in terms of which data centers and which locations and all of that stuff. Going into 2028 and beyond, I guess what I would say is the following. Look, I think we are seeing very strong I think we have a very strong business. We have a very strong balance sheet. And from that standpoint, our goal is first and foremost, we're investing in our growth to support that. And that means investing in R&D, investing in supply chain and capacity, investing alongside our partners to ensure that we have the capacity for all of those things that we talked about earlier that are necessary for this type of ramp. And then we are selectively investing with our lead partners where we see it's helpful to have, for example, the data center infrastructure identified way in advance, and that's multiple years in advance. And I think that's the right thing to do to ensure that we are jointly ensuring that there's the right infrastructure as our new chips become available. But we are being selective and strategic in how we do that, with the first principle being investing in our growth.

And for my follow-up, Lisa, one more on the competitive landscape. You know, many of your Frontier Lab customers have been working on their custom ASICs, and I'm curious, how do they conceptually make the choice between using ASICs versus AMD products? Like, what determines their allocation? Is it cost per token, power efficiency, software flexibility, time to deployment? I mean, just what are the puts and takes in that decision-making, and are there workloads where, you know, using an AMD GPU works better than the alternatives that they have? Thanks.

Sure, Vivek. So, look, I think we feel extremely good about where we're positioned in terms of our performance and our total cost of ownership that we're delivering with Helios. That is fundamentally the most important factor when we think about, you know, sort of deployment scale and deployments going forward. I think there was a significant investment that we've made in the rack-scale systems in ensuring that Helios really ramped nicely. The third quarter was the first quarter that we shipped MI-455 in Helios racks for revenue. I think this is a very major milestone. We have a big step up in Q4. We'll continue to ramp throughout 2027. And the key is for us to continue to show that TCO advantage across workloads. It is true that from a general purpose GPU standpoint that we have more fungibility as you think about various workloads that occur. There has been also very strong co-design. So beyond the MI450 series, we're working on MI500 and MI600 as well to ensure that our technology gets even more, let's call it, tuned to what the frontier labs need. So I think those are the key factors in terms of deployment choices.
Thank you, and the next question comes from the line of Joshua Buchalter with T.D. Cowan. Please proceed with your question.

Hey, guys. Thanks for taking my question, and congrats on the progress. I was wondering if you could give us insight into how we should be thinking about HBM costs impacting your model as the instinct business ramps. I think investors have been asking how your revenue per gigawatt contribution in the last year or so, your outlook has been so consistent in that $15 to $20 billion per gigawatt range, given what's going on with HBM pricing. Is that because early builds are fairly program-specific and pricing was agreed upon a long time ago? And again, as we think about that business longer term, do you have the ability to pass on these higher input costs even to your big three customers? Thank you.

Sure, Josh. So the way to think about it is, you know, as we ramp, we have had, let's call it, long-term agreements with some of our suppliers as well as some of our customers. But given where the memory market is, and not just the memory market, by the way, other component costs are, you know, also seeing some inflationary pressures in the sense of, you know, as there's more capex that's put into the overall supply chain environment. And we are also working with our customers to ensure that those costs are shared as we go forward. So from my perspective, back to the question that Vivek had, this is all about TCO and ensuring that from a tokens per dollar standpoint that we continue to offer very strong advantages for choosing AMD Instinct and our overall Helio system. And even with some of the inflationary pressures that are out there, we certainly believe that we are offering leading TCO for the AI workloads.

Thank you, Lisa. Then maybe for Gene, it was good to see OPEX come in light in the third and fourth quarter. It's been a sticking point for investors for a little bit. But I guess given how steep the revenue growth is expected to be in 2027, we're flying a little blind given you're kind of at more than 2x your target model. How should we think about OPEX growth in 27? And, you know, I guess while I'm in the neighborhood, you know, do you think you can hold your target gross margin range, you know, sort of that 55% floor as we move through the year and Helios continues to ramp? Thank you.

Yeah, Josh, thank you for the question. On the OPEX, as you said, we have been investing aggressively. What you're seeing is the investments are translating to accelerating revenue growth. We're seeing in 2026, we're actually quite pleased with 2026, our operating leverage. We're expanding revenue much faster than OPEX growth, which is driving the operating margin increase. If you think about the Q4 guide, we're guiding very significant revenue growth more than OPEX. That dynamic, we believe, will carry into 2027. Lisa talked about that we expect the whole company growing more than 80%. We should expect OPEX to grow less than the top-line revenue growth rate, less than half of the top-line revenue growth rate. So that will drive a very significant operating margin expansion in 2027. Going back to gross margin, we are actually very happy about where we are with our gross margin. In Q3, we are ramping MI450. Data center AI business is doing very well, actually better than our expectation when we got into the Q3 quarter. And in Q4, we're guiding sequentially revenue-growing. 50% for data center business, it's actually going to be the quarter data center AI business surpass server business. So we all know there's a margin, a little bit dilutive to corporate average, but The gross margin dollars are increasing very significantly. I think looking ahead of 2027, we actually think our data center business will be more than 80% of total company revenue. So the mix of a data center business is going to drive the company's gross margin significantly. The way to think about it is data center AI will continue to ramp through 2027. And the survey business is expected to double. So quarter over quarter, there may be variations because the mix of those businesses will be... A little bit different. In addition, embedded businesses are strengthening in 2027. I think that will also help our gross margin. Overall, when you put the whole business model together, what you should expect us to do is significant top-line revenue growth, significant gross profit expansion, and the OPEX growing less. And revenue growth, which will result in very significant operating margin expansion and profitability expansion.
Thank you. And the next question comes from the line of Timothy R. Corey with UBS. Please proceed with your question.

Thanks a lot. Lisa, I'm wondering if you can break down a little bit how data center is going to look like next year. You did revise server CPU up from up 70 to up more than 100%, but you're not being super specific about data center AI. So is the right way to think about it that the GPU business will still be bigger in dollars than the server CPU business, but not much? Is that the right way to think about the split? And then how to think about the, like, shape of the year. I know that the, you know, GP business is lumpy, but I imagine it's probably pretty, you know, rattable to the year. Is that kind of fair to think? Thanks.

Yeah, Tim, maybe let me break down a couple things. So first of all, we think 2027 is going to be a very strong momentum year for both the CPU business as well as the data center AI business. And, you know, when we gave you some of the markers, you should just consider them markers, right? So we've said the overall company will grow greater than 80 percent. And for the data center CPU business, we will about double. And for the data center AI business, it will significantly more than double.
